# Rachel Purcell Highlights New Zealand’s Nationwide Exercise Program for Bowel Cancer Patients

Rachel Purcell, Senior Research Fellow at the University of Otago and President of the New Zealand Society for Oncology, shared on LinkedIn:

“This is huge! A fantastic announcement from Bowel Cancer New Zealand this weekend.

Following the landmark clinical trial demonstrating that structured exercise programmes after chemotherapy can significantly improve survival in patients with colon cancer, Aotearoa New Zealand is leading the world in putting this evidence into practice.

Bowel Cancer NZ has announced the rollout of 34 sites across the country offering free, structured and supported exercise programmes for bowel cancer patients following chemotherapy.

This is exactly what we want to see – research findings translated into real, accessible benefits for patients.

And importantly, making sure that access isn’t determined by where you live or what you can afford.

An incredible initiative from the team at Bowel Cancer NZ, and something New Zealand should be very proud of!”

New Zealand Society for Oncology, shared on LinkedIn:

“A major NZSO2026 announcement from Bowel Cancer New Zealand highlights how evidence from cancer research is being translated into real-world supportive care across Aotearoa New Zealand.

The initiative reflects a growing focus on making evidence-based survivorship support accessible to patients in everyday clinical practice.

View the full interview“

# How One Brave Dog’s Tumor Trial Is Changing Cancer Treatment for Pets and Children

Image: Beth Wegerer By Beth Wegerer

Published March 3, 2026 5 min read

Alex Mladek/Shutterstock.com

Quick Take The Alternative Treatment That Saved Cla... How Clarice’s Success Can Help Chi... More About the WSU Clinical Trial

  * Washington State University is currently running clinical trials to test the effectiveness of immunotherapy injections in canine tumors.
  * Clarice was part of the trial and successfully had a tumor removed from her left wrist, avoiding typical leg amputation treatment.
  * Data from the canine trials is helping researchers at Seattle Children’s Hospital apply similar immunotherapy treatments to pediatric brain cancer patients.
  * Current trials, both for canines and humans, are ongoing.

When Jon and Dayla Culp received the news that their six-year-old Labrador retriever, Clarice, had a malignant tumor near her left wrist, the couple was devastated. Dayla had lost her sister, Darcy Klepec, to breast cancer less than two years earlier. Clarice had been a gift from Darcy.

## The Alternative Treatment That Saved Clarice

When the Culps met with the vet team at WSU, they learned about a new clinical trial being completed in partnership with Seattle Children’s Hospital. The focus of the trial was to test the efficacy of injecting an immune-stimulating agent directly into tumors in difficult-to-treat locations.

The clinical trial was only the first part of Clarice’s treatment plan. The WSU veterinary team combined the trial injection with surgery and radiation for a three-pronged approach. The goal was to eliminate the tumor without removing Clarice’s leg.

Image: veterinarian assistant in protective vest hold down prepare french bulldog to x-ray scanning.

Dogs in the WSU clinical trial often undergo radiation therapy as part of their treatment.

©Try_my_best/Shutterstock.com

For the Culp family, having Clarice back home and healthy is their biggest win. They are also grateful that their own dog’s cancer treatment and participation in the clinical trial might be able to help other people and pets. As Jon Culp noted in a recent article about the WSU clinical trial, “In the end, we wanted to do everything we could for Clarice. But knowing her treatment might help someone else someday made the decision feel even more meaningful.”

## How Clarice’s Success Can Help Children with Cancer

The data coming from the WSU trials is being shared with Seattle Children’s Hospital as part of a “comparative oncology” initiative. Canine tumors are biologically very similar to human pediatric brain tumors. The data from WSU’s canine trials is helping researchers design and refine the next phase of human clinical trials at Seattle Children’s Hospital.

WSU and Seattle Children’s Hospital worked together throughout 2024 and 2025 to develop the strategy to combine WSU’s veterinary expertise with the hospital’s pediatric CAR-T cell technology. That technology is being used in active clinical trials underway at the hospital.

Image: Seattle Cityscape Skyline Mount Rainier Aerial View, Washington, USA

Researchers at Seattle Children’s Hospital are using data from the WSU studies in human pediatric cancer treatment trials.

©Engel Ching/Shutterstock.com

## More About the WSU Clinical Trial

The WSU clinical trial, which is ongoing, focuses on local immunotherapy for solid and brain tumors in dogs. Dog owners interested in the program are invited to contact WSU.

Dogs participating in the trial must:

  * Have been diagnosed with an easily accessible soft tissue sarcoma with a minimum tumor size of 2 centimeters.
  * Be a suitable surgery candidate and have undergone all diagnostics considered standard of care.
  * Meet previously set parameters for bloodwork.

The long-term goal of this clinical trial is to add additional immunotherapy treatments to existing canine and human cancer care.

Image: Beth Wegerer

# Global Brain Cancer Trial to Open for Children in Australia and New Zealand

More children across Australia and New Zealand diagnosed with high-grade brain cancers will soon have the opportunity to take part in a world-leading international clinical trial, with the TarGeT trial set to open locally in 2026.

A national collaboration has come together to fund an innovative umbrella trial for childhood brain cancers.

More children across Australia and New Zealand diagnosed with high-grade brain cancers will soon have the opportunity to take part in a world-leading international clinical trial, with the TarGeT trial set to open locally in 2026.

The TarGeT trial is an innovative umbrella trial, a clinical trial design that tests multiple targeted treatments for a single disease. It will explore a range of treatments across different childhood brain cancers, with a key goal of ensuring the trial is accessible to children regardless of their specific tumour type.

The study will recruit patients across multiple hospital sites in both Australia and New Zealand, expanding access to cutting-edge research for families across the region.

# NIH's Definition of a Clinical Trial

This page provides information, tools, and resources about the definition of a clinical trial. Correctly identifying whether a study is considered by NIH to be a clinical trial is crucial to how you will:

## NIH Definition of a Clinical Trial

A research study in which one or more human subjects are prospectively assigned to one or more interventions (which may include placebo or other control) to evaluate the effects of those interventions on health-related biomedical or behavioral outcomes.

  1. Does the study involve human participants?
  2. Are the participants prospectively assigned to an intervention?
  3. Is the study designed to evaluate the effect of the intervention on the participants?
  4. Is the effect being evaluated a health-related biomedical or behavioral outcome?

LOS ANGELES — Keck Medicine of USC has launched a clinical trial testing the safety and tolerability of a new investigational treatment and its potential effects on preventing cartilage deterioration in people with knee osteoarthritis, the most common form of the disease. Malaghan Institute of Medical Research
Independent biomedical research institute in Wellington, New Zealand
The Malaghan Institute of Medical Research is an independent biomedical research institute based in Wellington, New Zealand. The Malaghan Institute specialises in the immune system, and how it can be harnessed to improve human health. Its key areas of research and discovery are cancer, allergic and inflammatory diseases, and infectious disease. In 2019, the institute began New Zealand's first clinical trial of CAR T-cell therapy, trialling a third-generation CAR T-cell therapy.

The concept of a Wellington-based, independent medical research institute was first proposed in the early 1960s. At that time, relatively little medical research was carried out in New Zealand due to a lack of facilities and support by hospital boards. Using funds from a trust established by the Wellington Medical Research Foundation and the Wellington Division of the Cancer Society, the Wellington Cancer and Medical Research Institute was opened on 26 July 1979, in rented premises in the Wellington School of Medicine.
